title: DefaultDispatchHook and IDispatchHook lack access control on onDispatch()
rejectionNote: Severity-auditor: no-op hook + future-code speculation. C4 discourages 'future code might do X' findings. IDispatchHook NatSpec already documents the call contract.
description: DefaultDispatchHook.onDispatch(address,uint256,bytes) is declared external with no access control. Any address can call it directly with arbitrary arguments. Because DefaultDispatchHook is a no-op, there is no direct impact today, but IDispatchHook (src/V2/interfaces/IDispatchHook.sol) does not document any required restriction either. The dispatch path assumes hook.onDispatch(minter, amount, extraData) is only reachable via ATokenDispatcherV2.dispatch, so future non-trivial hooks copying DefaultDispatchHook's pattern could be invoked directly by anyone, bypassing dispatcher context (paused state, reentrancy lock, onlyMinter) and letting callers forge the (minter, amount, extraData) tuple. Example risks: a future hook that pushes accounting updates ('amount of X was dispatched') could be poisoned by external callers spoofing values; a hook that rate-limits or meters per-dispatch actions can be driven from the outside at zero cost.
impact: Defense-in-depth and interface-contract issue. No current exploit, but the null-object pattern set by DefaultDispatchHook silently permits any future hook to be called out-of-context unless each hook author remembers to add msg.sender == dispatcher. The IDispatchHook interface doc ('Observation hook invoked by V2 dispatchers') does not mandate that guard, making the mis-step likely.
recommendation: Either (a) tighten the interface: document that onDispatch MUST restrict msg.sender to the dispatcher (or track the authorized dispatcher on the hook and enforce it); or (b) in ATokenDispatcherV2, store the hook-to-dispatcher binding so hooks can validate; or (c) at minimum add a require(msg.sender == <expected dispatcher>) in DefaultDispatchHook (with a setter) so the reference implementation models the correct pattern. Even though DefaultDispatchHook is a no-op, future hooks registered via setHook are likely to be authored by copying DefaultDispatchHook.
dedupNote: Unique. Targets the new V2 hook surface (DefaultDispatchHook / IDispatchHook) introduced in story-026. Not present in round-01/02/03 findings. Not covered by any knownIssues entry in registered-projects.json (yield-claim-NFT).
sanitizeNote: In V2 hook focus area (story-026 IDispatchHook/DefaultDispatchHook). Attack vector is permissionless caller invoking hook directly — NOT owner-driven. No match against project knownIssues (owner trust, FOT pattern, price ratchet, prior audit fixes).
classifyNote: C4 regular-audit Low/QA. No present-day asset risk: DefaultDispatchHook is a no-op so the missing access control has zero current impact. Entire risk surface depends on future hook authors copying the pattern, which falls under C4's 'speculation on future code without demonstrated root cause' (explicitly discouraged). Pure interface-contract / defense-in-depth issue. No protocol function or availability is impacted today. Confirm Low.
validityNote: Borderline future-code speculation pattern (entire risk surface depends on future hook authors copying DefaultDispatchHook). At Low/QA tier this pattern is tolerated as a hardening / interface-contract recommendation typical of QA bundles. Root cause is concretely present-day: the reference no-op hook ships with no access control AND the IDispatchHook interface doesn't mandate one, modeling the wrong pattern for future copy-paste. Keep as QA hardening item; do not promote above Low.
